tasks.prompt: Where is hosted scheduler registration implemented? Explain shared versus named options, the built-in startup/shutdown option defaults, and how a derived hosted service is retained when registrations overlap. Cite precise checked-in source ranges. Describe static behavior and its conditions; do not claim that a scheduler or job actually ran.

atoms.requirement: The ordinary AddQuartzHostedService overload delegates to the generic QuartzHostedService registration.
Generic registration uses ConfigureAll for a provided delegate and registers the hosted service.
Named registration validates a nonblank name and uses PostConfigure(name, configure), so named settings refine shared settings independent of registration order.
WaitForJobsToComplete defaults false, StartDelay null, AwaitApplicationStarted true and AutoStart true.

evidence.excerpt: public bool AutoStart { get; set; } = true;

atoms.requirement: AddHostedService searches implementation-type IHostedService registrations assignable to QuartzHostedService; adds singleton if absent, replaces the existing base type when requested type differs, otherwise keeps existing. Do not claim general deduplication of arbitrary factory/instance registrations or all competing subclasses.

tasks.prompt: Where does MicrosoftDependencyInjectionJobFactory resolve a job for a named scheduler? Explain the lookup order and exactly when it may construct a job without a dependency-injection scope. Cite precise checked-in source ranges. Describe static behavior and its conditions; do not claim that a scheduler or job actually ran.

atoms.requirement: Constructor derives schedulerKey from SchedulerScopedServiceProvider and permits the unscoped optimization only for the exact built-in factory type.
ResolveJob validates resolved job type, tries scheduler-keyed registration when a key exists, then unkeyed registration, then activator cache; FromContainer distinguishes these paths.
FindUnscopedConstructor rejects derived factories or a configured scope hook and requires an already loaded job type; decisions are cached by type per factory.

evidence.excerpt: private readonly ConcurrentDictionary<Type, ConstructorInvoker?> unscopedConstructors = new();

atoms.requirement: Unscoped eligibility requires a concrete non-value nongeneric-open IJob type with exactly one public parameterless constructor.
It also requires service-registration introspection and no unkeyed registration; a named scheduler also needs keyed introspection and no matching keyed registration. Otherwise retain the scoped path.

tasks.prompt: Trace a cron misfire policy from CronScheduleBuilder into CronTriggerImpl.UpdateAfterMisfire. Contrast SmartPolicy, DoNothing, and FireAndProceed, including calendar handling. Does that method itself execute a job? Cite precise checked-in source ranges. Describe static behavior and its conditions; do not claim that a scheduler or job actually ran.

atoms.requirement: Builder defaults to SmartPolicy, stores the typed policy as an integer, and copies it to the built CronTriggerImpl.
FireAndProceed maps to the FireOnceNow constant; DoNothing and SmartPolicy map to their corresponding constants.
UpdateAfterMisfire translates SmartPolicy to FireOnceNow.

DoNothing obtains a candidate using GetFireTimeAfter(current UTC time). While a candidate exists and a supplied calendar excludes it, it advances to the next candidate, exits if none exists, and clears a newly advanced candidate if its year exceeds YearToGiveUpSchedulingAt. It then assigns the resulting candidate or null to NextFireTimeUtc. With no calendar or an initially included candidate, the loop and its year check are skipped.
FireOnceNow sets NextFireTimeUtc to current time without the calendar-filter loop; this method changes trigger state, contains no job execution call, and does not prove actual firing.

tasks.prompt: Trace QuartzHostedService.StartAsync when some schedulers await application startup and others do not. Include scheduler creation, per-name options, AutoStart, delay, cancellation, and startup failure handling. Cite precise checked-in source ranges. Describe static behavior and its conditions; do not claim that a scheduler or job actually ran.

atoms.requirement: CreateSchedulers obtains the default factory and default options, then registered named keyed factories with per-name options; no schedulers produces configuration error.

StartAsync waits for creation then chooses the deferred path if any AutoStart+AwaitApplicationStarted scheduler exists; awaits already-completed startup tasks, otherwise allows host startup; the other path awaits inline starts.

Deferred path first starts non-waiting schedulers, waits for linked startup-cancellation or ApplicationStarted signal, then starts waiting schedulers only if startup was not canceled, using ApplicationStopping token.
StartSchedulers returns when application stopping; skips AutoStart=false and mismatched wait mode, and selects StartDelayed or Start. AutoStart=false does not skip creation.

StartAsync swallows OperationCanceledException observed in its try. Other exceptions observed there cause an awaited ShutdownSchedulers(CancellationToken.None); the original exception is rethrown if cleanup succeeds, while a cleanup failure escapes instead. An incomplete deferred startup task is not awaited by StartAsync, so its later failures are not covered by this catch. These paths establish no observed execution.

tasks.prompt: A change is proposed to how hosted schedulers stop. Identify the coordination points for repeated/concurrent StopAsync calls, startup in progress, dynamically added schedulers, waiting for jobs, and multiple shutdown failures. Bound the analysis to this hosted-service path. Cite precise checked-in source ranges. Describe static behavior and its conditions; do not claim that a scheduler or job actually ran.

atoms.requirement: StopAsync serializes creation of one cached stopTask; subsequent calls join it and do not substitute their token.

StopCore returns immediately if the hosted scheduler list is empty, without invoking ShutdownSchedulers or draining runtime tenants. Otherwise, if startupTask exists, it awaits Task.WhenAny(startupTask, an infinite delay using the stop token); it neither awaits the winning task nor cancels startup itself. Its finally invokes ShutdownSchedulers with the first stop caller's token even when that token is canceled.
ShutdownSchedulers atomically takes the hosted list and adds runtime live schedulers with options fetched by scheduler name.

Once scheduler discovery and named-options retrieval have completed successfully, ShutdownSchedulers initiates every collected scheduler's Shutdown call before awaiting the resulting tasks. It passes each scheduler's WaitForJobsToComplete and the common cancellation token; synchronous exceptions from invoking Shutdown or converting its ValueTask become failed tasks. A failure while collecting runtime schedulers/options occurs outside these per-scheduler catches and can prevent this loop.

Each created shutdown task is awaited with exceptions collected, and a nonempty collection produces AggregateException. A change to invocation or awaiting order can alter overlapping waits and the existing attempt-all/error-aggregation behavior. This is static behavior of the hosted-service path, not proof of shutdown or job completion; no assertion that arbitrary proposed changes must preserve this policy is required.

tasks.prompt: A change is proposed to job creation and cleanup in MicrosoftDependencyInjectionJobFactory. Review ownership and failure handling for scoped container-resolved jobs, factory-activated jobs, unscoped jobs, and derived factories replacing JobScope.State. What prevents duplicate disposal of its own scope state? Cite precise checked-in source ranges. Describe static behavior and its conditions; do not claim that a scheduler or job actually ran.

atoms.requirement: Scoped creation opens a scope, invokes ConfigureScope before ResolveJob, and records disposeJob = !fromContainer in ScopeState. Keyed or unkeyed container resolution sets fromContainer=true, so this factory does not directly dispose that job; it disposes the scope and leaves job ownership to container registration/lifetime rules. Factory activation sets fromContainer=false, so ScopeState attempts direct job disposal before disposing the scope.

If ConfigureScope or ResolveJob fails after the scope was opened, CreateJobInstance attempts scope disposal itself; if disposal succeeds it rethrows the original failure via ExceptionDispatchInfo, but a disposal failure replaces it. CreateScope itself is outside this try. A failure before JobScope is returned cannot rely on normal ReturnJob. Separately, the inherited CreateJob calls ReturnJob when ApplyProperties fails after a JobScope exists; it logs cleanup failure and preserves that property-application exception.

Successful unscoped construction returns the Unscoped sentinel state. Constructor exceptions become a faulted ValueTask<JobScope>. ReturnJob recognizing this sentinel calls DisposeIfDisposable on the job: async disposal is preferred, otherwise synchronous disposal is used, and nondisposable jobs are left alone. This branch has no ScopeState-style duplicate-disposal guard.

ReturnJob delegates its own ScopeState to DisposeAsync. For state that is neither ScopeState nor the Unscoped sentinel, it leaves the job untouched and calls DisposeIfDisposable on the replacement state, preferring async disposal and doing nothing for nondisposable state. A derived factory must preserve/cascade original cleanup through its replacement state or override ReturnJob to perform that teardown.

ScopeState uses Interlocked.Exchange(ref disposed, 1) before cleanup so only the first caller attempts disposal; later callers return immediately, do not join that attempt, and cannot retry a failed attempt. Only factory-activated jobs are passed to DisposeIfDisposable. The scope is disposed in finally, preferring IAsyncDisposable and otherwise IDisposable; this is an attempt, not a guarantee of successful cleanup. A scope-disposal exception can replace a job-disposal exception.

Accept equivalent precise implementation ranges. A precise full-method range is sufficient for a method-local negative claim such as no job invocation.
